# Introduction and hypotheses

Insulin resistance in skeletal muscle precedes type 2 diabetes (T2D), and aging is itself a
major risk factor for both. Jin et al. (2011) profiled vastus lateralis biopsies from
normoglycemic people with or without a family history (FH) of T2D and from people with T2D,
and reported that increased serum response factor (SRF) activity marks insulin resistance.
The Hallmarks of Aging (López-Otín et al., 2013) predicts that age-associated changes should
involve mitochondrial dysfunction, deregulated nutrient sensing, altered intercellular
communication (inflammation), and loss of proteostasis.

Hypotheses tested here:

* **H1.** Unsupervised clustering of muscle transcriptomes separates samples by a biological
  factor (sex, diabetes status, or age), not at random.
* **H2.** Sex is the strongest single source of transcriptome-wide variation, driven by
  sex-chromosome genes.
* **H3.** A set of genes is correlated with age, and these genes are enriched for
  Hallmark-of-Aging processes (mitochondria / oxidative phosphorylation, extracellular matrix,
  inflammation).
* **H4.** Because the diabetic group is older than the other groups, part of any apparent "age
  signature" is confounded by diabetes; this must be tested explicitly.

# Data and preprocessing

* **Expression:** `BE700_human_expression_1.csv`, Affymetrix HG-U133 Plus 2.0 (GPL570),
  summarized to gene symbols and already log-normalized (no further normalization applied).
* **Phenotypes:** `BE700_human_pheno_1.csv`, the GEO series matrix sample table; the
  informative columns are those ending in `:ch1`.

```{r load}
expr_raw <- read.csv("data/BE700_human_expression_1.csv", check.names = FALSE,
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
genes <- expr_raw[[1]]
keep  <- !is.na(genes) & genes != ""
expr  <- as.matrix(expr_raw[keep, -1]); rownames(expr) <- genes[keep]

ph_raw <- read.csv("data/BE700_human_pheno_1.csv", check.names = FALSE,
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
num <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))   # "missing value" -> NA
ph <- data.frame(
  sample   = ph_raw$geo_accession,
  title    = ph_raw$title,
  sex      = factor(ph_raw[["gender:ch1"]]),
  age      = num(ph_raw[["age (years):ch1"]]),
  bmi      = num(ph_raw[["body mass index (kg/m2):ch1"]]),
  whr      = num(ph_raw[["waist hip ratio:ch1"]]),
  hba1c    = num(ph_raw[["hemoglobin a1c:ch1"]]),
  fglu     = num(ph_raw[["fasting glucose (iv0gavg):ch1"]]),
  finsulin = num(ph_raw[["fasting insulin (iv0inavg):ch1"]]),
  si       = num(ph_raw[["si:ch1"]]),
  glu2h    = num(ph_raw[["2 hour glucose (ogtt):ch1"]]),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ph$group <- factor(sub("^Muscle-", "", sub("-[0-9]+$", "", ph$title)),
                   levels = c("FamilyHistoryNegative", "FamilyHistoryPositive", "Diabetes"),
                   labels = c("FH-", "FH+", "T2D"))
ph$label    <- paste0(c("FH-" = "N", "FH+" = "P", "T2D" = "D")[as.character(ph$group)],
                      sub(".*-", "", ph$title))      # short plot labels, e.g. D3, N12
ph$diabetes <- factor(ph$group == "T2D", labels = c("No", "Yes"))
rownames(ph) <- ph$sample

stopifnot(identical(colnames(expr), ph$sample))       # QC: sample order matches
dim(expr)
```

The matrix has **`r nrow(expr)` genes x `r ncol(expr)` samples**; one row with an empty gene
name was removed. Sample order matches the phenotype table.

```{r pheno-table}
tab <- aggregate(cbind(age, bmi, hba1c, si) ~ group, data = ph,
                 FUN = function(x) round(mean(x), 1), na.action = na.pass)
tab$n      <- as.vector(table(ph$group))
tab$female <- as.vector(table(ph$group, ph$sex)[, "female"])
knitr::kable(tab[, c("group", "n", "female", "age", "bmi", "hba1c", "si")],
             caption = "Cohort by group (means; SI = insulin sensitivity).")
kruskal.test(age ~ group, data = ph)
colSums(is.na(ph[, c("whr", "si", "glu2h")]))
```

**Data issues found.** (i) The T2D group is older than the FH- and FH+ groups (age differs
by group, Kruskal-Wallis above), so age and diabetes are confounded (H4). (ii) OGTT values are
missing for all T2D subjects, SI for two, and waist-hip ratio for one (stored as the string
"missing value"). (iii) One FH- subject has BMI 20 but WHR 1.36, the cohort maximum, which is
probably a data-entry error; WHR is therefore not used for inference.

## Quality control

```{r qc-box, fig.height=3.2, fig.cap="Per-sample expression distributions (log scale). Distributions are comparable, so no further normalization was applied."}
ord <- order(ph$group)
boxplot(expr[, ord], outline = FALSE, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.5, names = ph$label[ord],
        col = c("grey85", "lightblue", "salmon")[ph$group[ord]], ylab = "log expression")
legend("topright", fill = c("grey85", "lightblue", "salmon"), legend = levels(ph$group),
       cex = 0.7, horiz = TRUE, bty = "n")
```

```{r qc-sex, fig.height=3.4, fig.width=4.5, out.width="55%", fig.cap="Sex check: XIST (X-inactivation) versus RPS4Y1 (Y-linked)."}
sexchk <- data.frame(XIST = expr["XIST", ], RPS4Y1 = expr["RPS4Y1", ], sex = ph$sex)
ggplot(sexchk, aes(XIST, RPS4Y1, colour = sex)) + geom_point(size = 2)
pred_sex <- ifelse(sexchk$XIST > 11 & sexchk$RPS4Y1 < 12, "female",
             ifelse(sexchk$XIST < 11 & sexchk$RPS4Y1 > 12, "male", "ambiguous"))
mm <- pred_sex != as.character(ph$sex)
knitr::kable(data.frame(sample = ph$label, reported = ph$sex, XIST = sexchk$XIST,
                        RPS4Y1 = sexchk$RPS4Y1, expression_says = pred_sex)[mm, ],
             digits = 1, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Samples whose expression disagrees with reported sex.")
```

Reported sex agrees with XIST/RPS4Y1 expression for `r sum(!mm)` of `r nrow(ph)` samples.
`r paste(ph$label[mm & pred_sex == "male"], collapse = ", ")` is reported female but expresses
Y-linked genes and lacks XIST, so it is most likely a mislabeled male.
`r paste(ph$label[mm & pred_sex == "ambiguous"], collapse = ", ")` expresses **both** XIST and
Y-linked genes at high levels; this is consistent with a mixed / contaminated sample (or, less
likely, a 47,XXY karyotype). The same subject has the implausible WHR noted above, so this record
is treated with suspicion. Both samples are kept with their reported labels in the main analysis
and excluded in a sensitivity analysis (Section 6).

## Outlier samples

```{r qc-outlier, fig.height=3, fig.cap="Median Pearson correlation of each sample with all other samples. Red: below Q1 - 1.5 IQR."}
cc <- cor(expr)
medcor <- apply(cc, 2, function(v) median(v[v < 1]))
thr <- quantile(medcor, 0.25) - 1.5 * IQR(medcor)
outl <- ph$label[medcor < thr]
o2 <- order(medcor)
barplot(medcor[o2], names.arg = ph$label[o2], las = 2, cex.names = 0.5,
        col = ifelse(medcor[o2] < thr, "firebrick", "grey70"), ylim = c(0.75, 0.9), xpd = FALSE,
        ylab = "median r with other samples")
abline(h = thr, lty = 2)
excl <- ph$sample[medcor < thr | mm]   # outliers + sex-discordant samples
```

The median between-sample correlation is only `r round(median(medcor), 3)`, so the arrays are
noisy relative to typical RNA-seq data. Outlier samples: `r if (length(outl)) paste(outl, collapse = ", ") else "none"`.

# Heatmap of the muscle transcriptome

Genes were ranked by variance across samples and the 1,000 most variable were kept; each gene
was z-scored across samples. Samples and genes were clustered hierarchically (Euclidean
distance, Ward.D2 linkage).

```{r hm-prep}
v     <- apply(expr, 1, var)
top   <- names(sort(v, decreasing = TRUE))[1:1000]
z     <- t(scale(t(expr[top, ])))
ann   <- data.frame(Sex = ph$sex, Group = ph$group, Age = ph$age, BMI = ph$bmi,
                    row.names = ph$sample)
ann_col <- list(Sex = c(female = "#E7298A", male = "#1B9E77"),
                Group = c("FH-" = "grey70", "FH+" = "#7570B3", "T2D" = "#D95F02"))
```

```{r hm-all, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Top 1,000 most variable genes, z-scored, Ward.D2 clustering."}
pheatmap(z, show_rownames = FALSE, labels_col = ph$label, fontsize_col = 6,
         annotation_col = ann, annotation_colors = ann_col,
         clustering_method = "ward.D2", treeheight_row = 0,
         breaks = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 101),
         color = colorRampPalette(c("navy", "white", "firebrick3"))(100))
```

To see what lies under the sex signal, sex-associated genes were identified with a Welch
t-test (BH q < 0.05 and |mean difference| > 1 log unit) and removed, and the heatmap was redrawn
on the 1,000 most variable remaining genes.

```{r sex-genes}
tt <- apply(expr, 1, function(g) t.test(g ~ ph$sex)$p.value)
dm <- rowMeans(expr[, ph$sex == "male"]) - rowMeans(expr[, ph$sex == "female"])
sex_genes <- names(which(p.adjust(tt, "BH") < 0.05 & abs(dm) > 1))
length(sex_genes); head(sort(sex_genes), 25)
expr_ns <- expr[setdiff(rownames(expr), sex_genes), ]
top_ns  <- names(sort(apply(expr_ns, 1, var), decreasing = TRUE))[1:1000]
z_ns    <- t(scale(t(expr_ns[top_ns, ])))
```

```{r hm-nosex, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Top 1,000 most variable genes after removing sex-associated genes."}
pheatmap(z_ns, show_rownames = FALSE, labels_col = ph$label, fontsize_col = 6,
         annotation_col = ann, annotation_colors = ann_col,
         clustering_method = "ward.D2", treeheight_row = 0,
         breaks = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 101),
         color = colorRampPalette(c("navy", "white", "firebrick3"))(100))
```

# Clustering patients

Both k-means (25 random starts) and hierarchical clustering (Ward.D2) were applied to the
samples, on the z-scored top-1,000 genes with and without sex-associated genes. The number
of clusters was chosen by average silhouette width for k = 2 to 6, and agreement between
methods was measured with the adjusted Rand index (ARI).

```{r cluster}
ari <- function(a, b) {                       # adjusted Rand index
  tab <- table(a, b); n <- sum(tab); c2 <- function(x) sum(choose(x, 2))
  e <- c2(rowSums(tab)) * c2(colSums(tab)) / choose(n, 2)
  (c2(tab) - e) / ((c2(rowSums(tab)) + c2(colSums(tab))) / 2 - e)
}
run_clusters <- function(zmat) {
  X  <- t(zmat); d <- dist(X); hc <- hclust(d, "ward.D2")
  sil <- sapply(2:6, function(k) {
    km <- kmeans(X, k, nstart = 25)
    c(kmeans = mean(silhouette(km$cluster, d)[, 3]),
      hclust = mean(silhouette(cutree(hc, k), d)[, 3]))
  })
  colnames(sil) <- paste0("k=", 2:6)
  list(X = X, d = d, hc = hc, sil = sil)
}
cl_all <- run_clusters(z); cl_ns <- run_clusters(z_ns)
round(cl_all$sil, 3); round(cl_ns$sil, 3)
```

```{r cluster-assign}
k_all <- which.max(cl_all$sil["kmeans", ]) + 1
k_ns  <- which.max(cl_ns$sil["kmeans", ]) + 1
ph$km_all <- factor(kmeans(cl_all$X, k_all, nstart = 25)$cluster)
ph$hc_all <- factor(cutree(cl_all$hc, k_all))
ph$km_ns  <- factor(kmeans(cl_ns$X, k_ns, nstart = 25)$cluster)
ph$hc_ns  <- factor(cutree(cl_ns$hc, k_ns))
c(k_all = k_all, ARI_all = round(ari(ph$km_all, ph$hc_all), 2),
  k_nosex = k_ns, ARI_nosex = round(ari(ph$km_ns, ph$hc_ns), 2))
table(kmeans_all = ph$km_all, sex = ph$sex)
table(kmeans_nosex = ph$km_ns, group = ph$group)
```

## Are clusters enriched for phenotypes?

Categorical phenotypes were tested with Fisher's exact test and continuous phenotypes with
the Kruskal-Wallis test; p-values were BH-adjusted within each clustering.

```{r enrich}
enrich <- function(cl) {
  cat_v <- c(sex = "sex", group = "group", diabetes = "diabetes")
  con_v <- c(age = "age", BMI = "bmi", HbA1c = "hba1c", SI = "si",
             fasting_insulin = "finsulin", fasting_glucose = "fglu")
  p <- c(sapply(cat_v, function(v) fisher.test(table(cl, ph[[v]]))$p.value),
         sapply(con_v, function(v) kruskal.test(ph[[v]] ~ cl)$p.value))
  data.frame(phenotype = names(p), p = signif(p, 2), q_BH = signif(p.adjust(p, "BH"), 2))
}
en <- merge(setNames(enrich(ph$km_all), c("phenotype", "p_all", "q_all")),
            setNames(enrich(ph$km_ns),  c("phenotype", "p_nosex", "q_nosex")))
knitr::kable(en[order(en$q_all), ], row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Phenotype enrichment of k-means clusters, all genes vs sex genes removed.")
write.csv(en, "results/cluster_enrichment.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r cluster-box, fig.height=3.2, fig.cap="Phenotypes by k-means cluster (sex-associated genes removed)."}
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("age", "bmi", "hba1c", "si"), function(v)
  data.frame(cluster = ph$km_ns, variable = v, value = ph[[v]])))
ggplot(long, aes(cluster, value, fill = cluster)) + geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 0.8) + facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

**Do male and female patients form distinct clusters?** With all genes, the k-means partition
(k = `r k_all`) against sex has Fisher p = `r signif(en$p_all[en$phenotype=="sex"], 2)`.
After sex-associated genes are removed, that association becomes
p = `r signif(en$p_nosex[en$phenotype=="sex"], 2)`.

# Genes correlated with age

For every gene, the Pearson and Spearman correlation with age was computed across all 50
subjects, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR. Because the T2D group is older (H4), two robustness
checks were added: (a) a linear model `expression ~ age + sex + diabetes` fitted to every gene,
and (b) the correlation re-computed in the 40 non-diabetic subjects only.

```{r age-cor}
cor_test_vec <- function(M, x, method = "pearson") {
  r <- as.vector(cor(t(M), x, method = method, use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))
  n <- sum(!is.na(x)); tstat <- r * sqrt((n - 2) / (1 - r^2))
  p <- 2 * pt(-abs(tstat), n - 2)
  data.frame(gene = rownames(M), r = r, p = p, q = p.adjust(p, "BH"))
}
pear <- cor_test_vec(expr, ph$age, "pearson")
spear <- cor_test_vec(expr, ph$age, "spearman")
nd <- ph$diabetes == "No"
pear_nd <- cor_test_vec(expr[, nd], ph$age[nd], "pearson")

# Vectorized OLS: expression ~ age + sex + diabetes, t-test on the age coefficient
X <- model.matrix(~ age + sex + diabetes, ph)
B <- solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, t(expr)))
res <- t(expr) - X %*% B
s2 <- colSums(res^2) / (nrow(X) - ncol(X))
se_age <- sqrt(s2 * solve(crossprod(X))["age", "age"])
t_age <- B["age", ] / se_age
p_lm <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_age), nrow(X) - ncol(X))

age_tab <- data.frame(gene = pear$gene, r_pearson = pear$r, q_pearson = pear$q,
                      r_spearman = spear$r, q_spearman = spear$q,
                      r_nondiabetic = pear_nd$r, p_nondiabetic = pear_nd$p,
                      beta_age_adj = B["age", ], q_adj = p.adjust(p_lm, "BH"))
age_tab <- age_tab[order(pear$p), ]
write.csv(age_tab, "results/age_correlation_all_genes.csv", row.names = FALSE)

sig <- c(pearson_q05 = sum(age_tab$q_pearson < 0.05),
         spearman_q05 = sum(age_tab$q_spearman < 0.05),
         adjusted_q05 = sum(age_tab$q_adj < 0.05),
         nondiabetic_p001 = sum(age_tab$p_nondiabetic < 0.001),
         pearson_p001 = sum(pear$p < 0.001))
sig
```

```{r age-select}
# Age-gene set: Pearson FDR < 0.05; fall back to the top 100 by p if fewer than 30 pass
age_genes <- if (sig["pearson_q05"] >= 30) age_tab$gene[age_tab$q_pearson < 0.05] else
  head(age_tab$gene, 100)
age_rule  <- if (sig["pearson_q05"] >= 30) "Pearson FDR < 0.05" else "top 100 by Pearson p"
robust    <- age_tab$gene[age_tab$gene %in% age_genes & age_tab$q_adj < 0.1 &
                          sign(age_tab$r_nondiabetic) == sign(age_tab$r_pearson)]
c(n_age_genes = length(age_genes), n_up = sum(age_tab$r_pearson[age_tab$gene %in% age_genes] > 0),
  n_robust = length(robust))
knitr::kable(head(age_tab[, c("gene", "r_pearson", "q_pearson", "r_spearman",
                              "r_nondiabetic", "q_adj")], 20),
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Top 20 age-correlated genes. q_adj: FDR for age in expression ~ age + sex + diabetes.")
```

The age-gene set (`r age_rule`) contains **`r length(age_genes)` genes**; `r length(robust)` of
them stay significant after adjusting for sex and diabetes (q < 0.1) and keep the same
direction in non-diabetic subjects.

## Heatmap of age-correlated genes

```{r hm-age, fig.height=6.5, fig.cap="Age-correlated genes; samples ordered by age (left = youngest). Genes clustered."}

za <- t(scale(t(expr[age_genes, oa])))
pheatmap(za, cluster_cols = FALSE, show_rownames = length(age_genes) <= 60,
         fontsize_row = 5, labels_col = paste0(ph$label[oa], " (", ph$age[oa], ")"),
         fontsize_col = 5, annotation_col = ann, annotation_colors = ann_col,
         clustering_method = "ward.D2", treeheight_row = 20,
         breaks = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 101),

```

```{r age-scatter, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Top 9 age-correlated genes; T2D subjects in orange. Lines: linear fit on all subjects."}
top9 <- head(age_tab$gene, 9)
sc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(top9, function(g) data.frame(
  gene = sprintf("%s (r = %.2f)", g, age_tab$r_pearson[age_tab$gene == g]),
  age = ph$age, expr = expr[g, ], group = ph$group)))
sc$gene <- factor(sc$gene, levels = unique(sc$gene))
ggplot(sc, aes(age, expr)) + geom_point(aes(colour = group), size = 1.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ann_col$Group) +

```

```{r age-bar, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Top 30 age-correlated genes: Pearson r, all subjects vs non-diabetic subjects only."}
t30 <- head(age_tab, 30)
bar <- rbind(data.frame(gene = t30$gene, r = t30$r_pearson, set = "all (n = 50)"),
             data.frame(gene = t30$gene, r = t30$r_nondiabetic, set = "non-diabetic (n = 40)"))
bar$gene <- factor(bar$gene, levels = rev(t30$gene))
ggplot(bar, aes(r, gene, fill = set)) + geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.75) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + labs(x = "Pearson r with age", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6), legend.position = "top")
```

# Principal component analysis

PCA (`prcomp`) was run on all `r nrow(expr)` genes, each centered to mean zero but not scaled
(the data are already on a log scale, so unscaled PCA keeps high-variance genes influential).
It was repeated after removing sex-associated genes. Each point is labeled with the subject
code (N = FH-, P = FH+, D = T2D, followed by the GEO sample number within the group).

```{r pca}
pca    <- prcomp(t(expr), center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
pca_ns <- prcomp(t(expr_ns), center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
ve     <- 100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
ve_ns  <- 100 * pca_ns$sdev^2 / sum(pca_ns$sdev^2)
round(rbind(all = ve[1:6], no_sex = ve_ns[1:6]), 1)
pcd <- cbind(ph, pca$x[, 1:6]); pcd_ns <- cbind(ph, pca_ns$x[, 1:6])
```

```{r pca-sex, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="PCA of all genes, colored by sex, shaped by group."}
ggplot(pcd, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = sex, shape = group)) + geom_point(size = 2.3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), size = 2.4, max.overlaps = 50, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ann_col$Sex) +
  labs(x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", ve[1]), y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", ve[2]))
```

```{r pca-age, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="PCA after removing sex-associated genes, colored by age, shaped by group."}
ggplot(pcd_ns, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = age, shape = group)) + geom_point(size = 2.3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), size = 2.4, max.overlaps = 50, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", ve_ns[1]), y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", ve_ns[2]))
```

**Sensitivity analysis.** The first PCs are pulled by a few individual samples (e.g. D10 alone
drives PC2). PCA was therefore repeated without the outlier and sex-discordant samples
(`r paste(ph$label[ph$sample %in% excl], collapse = ", ")`), using the 1,000 most variable
non-sex genes, each scaled to unit variance so no single gene dominates.

```{r pca-sens, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="Sensitivity PCA: outlier and sex-discordant samples removed, top 1,000 variable non-sex genes, scaled. Colored by group, size by BMI."}
keep_s  <- !(ph$sample %in% excl)
pca_s   <- prcomp(t(expr_ns[top_ns, keep_s]), center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
ve_s    <- 100 * pca_s$sdev^2 / sum(pca_s$sdev^2)
pcd_s   <- cbind(ph[keep_s, ], pca_s$x[, 1:6])
ggplot(pcd_s, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = group, size = bmi)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), size = 2.4, max.overlaps = 50, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ann_col$Group) + scale_size(range = c(1.2, 4)) +
  labs(x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", ve_s[1]), y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", ve_s[2]))
```

```{r pc-assoc}
pc_assoc <- function(d) {
  vars <- c("age", "bmi", "hba1c", "si", "finsulin")
  out <- sapply(paste0("PC", 1:6), function(pc) c(
    sex = wilcox.test(d[[pc]] ~ d$sex)$p.value,
    group = kruskal.test(d[[pc]] ~ d$group)$p.value,
    sapply(vars, function(v) cor.test(d[[pc]], d[[v]], method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)$p.value)))
  signif(out, 2)
}
knitr::kable(pc_assoc(pcd), caption = "P-values: PCs (all genes) vs phenotypes (Wilcoxon / Kruskal-Wallis / Spearman).")
knitr::kable(pc_assoc(pcd_ns), caption = "P-values: PCs (sex-associated genes removed) vs phenotypes.")
knitr::kable(pc_assoc(pcd_s), caption = "P-values: sensitivity PCA (outliers removed) vs phenotypes.")
```

```{r pc-loadings}
ld <- pca_ns$rotation
data.frame(PC1_top_pos = names(head(sort(ld[, 1], decreasing = TRUE), 10)),
           PC1_top_neg = names(head(sort(ld[, 1]), 10)),
           PC2_top_pos = names(head(sort(ld[, 2], decreasing = TRUE), 10)),
           PC2_top_neg = names(head(sort(ld[, 2]), 10)))
```

# Additional analysis: insulin sensitivity and diabetes

As an exploratory extension, every gene was correlated (Spearman) with insulin sensitivity
(SI, n = 48), and T2D was compared with FH- subjects (Welch t-test). Genes from Jin et al.'s
SRF story (SRF, its co-activator MKL1/MRTF-A, and the SRF targets ACTA2, FHL1, VCL, CNN2) are
checked individually.

```{r si}
si_ok <- !is.na(ph$si)
si_cor <- cor_test_vec(expr[, si_ok], ph$si[si_ok], "spearman")
si_cor <- si_cor[order(si_cor$p), ]
c(si_q05 = sum(si_cor$q < 0.05), si_p001 = sum(si_cor$p < 0.001))
write.csv(si_cor, "results/si_correlation_all_genes.csv", row.names = FALSE)

d_vs_n <- ph$group %in% c("T2D", "FH-")
grp <- droplevels(ph$group[d_vs_n])
de_p <- apply(expr[, d_vs_n], 1, function(g) t.test(g ~ grp)$p.value)
de_fc <- rowMeans(expr[, ph$group == "T2D"]) - rowMeans(expr[, ph$group == "FH-"])
de <- data.frame(gene = names(de_p), log_diff_T2D_vs_FHneg = de_fc, p = de_p,
                 q = p.adjust(de_p, "BH"))[order(de_p), ]
c(de_q05 = sum(de$q < 0.05), de_p001 = sum(de$p < 0.001))
write.csv(de, "results/T2D_vs_FHneg.csv", row.names = FALSE)

srf <- intersect(c("SRF", "MKL1", "MRTFA", "ACTA2", "FHL1", "VCL", "CNN2", "MYH11"), rownames(expr))
knitr::kable(data.frame(gene = srf,
  r_SI = si_cor$r[match(srf, si_cor$gene)], p_SI = si_cor$p[match(srf, si_cor$gene)],
  diff_T2D_FHneg = de$log_diff_T2D_vs_FHneg[match(srf, de$gene)],
  p_T2D_FHneg = de$p[match(srf, de$gene)]), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "SRF pathway genes: correlation with SI and T2D vs FH- difference.")
c(overlap_age_SI = length(intersect(age_genes, head(si_cor$gene, length(age_genes)))))
```

```{r volcano, fig.height=4, fig.cap="T2D vs FH-: difference in mean log expression vs significance."}
de$lab <- ifelse(rank(de$p) <= 15, de$gene, "")
ggplot(de, aes(log_diff_T2D_vs_FHneg, -log10(p))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = de[de$lab != "", ], colour = "#D95F02", size = 1.2) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = lab), size = 2.5, max.overlaps = 30) +
  labs(x = "mean log expression, T2D minus FH-", y = "-log10 p")
```

# Gene lists for DAVID (Part III)

Gene lists are written to `results/` for upload to DAVID
(<https://davidbioinformatics.nih.gov>, Functional Annotation, identifier type OFFICIAL_GENE_SYMBOL,
species *Homo sapiens*, background = all genes on the array), where KEGG pathways and GO
Biological Process terms are examined. DAVID is a web tool, so this step is run by hand on the
exported lists; its results (top KEGG / GO terms with FDR) will be added here after the in-class
discussion of Part III.

```{r export}
up   <- age_tab$gene[age_tab$gene %in% age_genes & age_tab$r_pearson > 0]
down <- age_tab$gene[age_tab$gene %in% age_genes & age_tab$r_pearson < 0]
writeLines(up,   "results/DAVID_age_up.txt")
writeLines(down, "results/DAVID_age_down.txt")
writeLines(robust, "results/DAVID_age_robust.txt")
writeLines(head(si_cor$gene, 200), "results/DAVID_SI_top200.txt")
writeLines(rownames(expr), "results/DAVID_background.txt")
# cluster marker genes: top 100 genes by t-statistic for each no-sex k-means cluster
for (k in levels(ph$km_ns)) {
  tk <- apply(expr_ns, 1, function(g) t.test(g[ph$km_ns == k], g[ph$km_ns != k])$statistic)
  writeLines(names(head(sort(tk, decreasing = TRUE), 100)),
             sprintf("results/DAVID_cluster%s_up.txt", k))
}
c(age_up = length(up), age_down = length(down), robust = length(robust))
```

# Discussion

**Main result: the muscle transcriptome has little strong, unsupervised structure.** The
heatmap of the 1,000 most variable genes shows no clear sample blocks, average silhouette widths
are about 0.02 for every k from 2 to 6 (values near 0 mean no real cluster separation), and
k-means and hierarchical clustering only partly agree (ARI = `r round(ari(ph$km_all, ph$hc_all), 2)`).
The best k-means split (k = 2) is not enriched for sex, group, diabetes, or age after FDR
correction; the strongest nominal signal is insulin sensitivity (SI, p = `r en$p_all[en$phenotype=="SI"]`)
with BMI and fasting insulin close behind. H1 is therefore only weakly supported: whatever
separates the clusters is related to insulin resistance / adiposity rather than to the
recorded diagnostic groups.

**Unexpected finding 1: sex is not the dominant axis (H2 rejected).** Only `r length(sex_genes)`
genes differ strongly by sex, almost all on the X/Y chromosomes (XIST, TSIX, RPS4Y1, DDX3Y,
KDM5D, UTY, USP9Y, ZFY, EIF1AY), plus a few autosomal adipose-related genes (LEP, ADH1B, CD24),
which probably reflect sex differences in intramuscular fat. With ~22,000 genes these 19 genes
contribute almost nothing to PCA or clustering, so removing them changed neither result. Men and
women do not form distinct clusters.

**Unexpected finding 2: data-quality problems.** Two of 50 samples disagree with their reported
sex (P25 looks male; N1 expresses both XIST and Y genes and also has an implausible WHR), and two
samples (`r paste(outl, collapse = ", ")`) are global outliers that drive the leading PCs. In the
full PCA, PC1 explains only `r round(ve[1], 1)`% of the variance and its top loadings (ribosomal,
hemoglobin, heat-shock genes) look like tissue-composition or RNA-quality effects rather than
biology. After removing these samples and scaling genes, PC2 becomes associated with SI
(p = `r pc_assoc(pcd_s)["si", "PC2"]`) and fasting insulin, which matches the clustering result.

**Age-associated genes (H3, H4).** No gene passes FDR < 0.05 for age (the best q is about 0.05),
which is expected with n = 50 and a 21 to 67-year age range, so the top 100 genes by p-value are
used as an exploratory set. Their direction is informative: many of the strongest
age-*decreasing* genes encode mitochondrial and energy-metabolism proteins (MFF, mitochondrial
fission; DLAT, pyruvate dehydrogenase; MDH2, TCA cycle; ATP5F1, ATP synthase; MRPL15,
mitochondrial ribosome), which fits the "mitochondrial dysfunction" hallmark of aging. However,
the correlations weaken in the 40 non-diabetic subjects and only `r length(robust)` gene
(`r paste(robust, collapse = ", ")`) remains significant after adjusting for sex and diabetes.
Because the T2D group is about 12 years older, part of the apparent age signature is a diabetes
signature, so H4 is supported. DAVID on the age-down list is the planned test of whether the
mitochondrial theme is statistically enriched.

**Reproduction of Jin et al.** SRF and its co-activator MKL1 are negatively correlated with
insulin sensitivity (SRF r = `r round(si_cor$r[si_cor$gene=="SRF"], 2)`, MKL1
r = `r round(si_cor$r[si_cor$gene=="MKL1"], 2)`), and SRF and the SRF targets VCL and CNN2 are
higher in T2D than in FH- subjects (nominal p < 0.05). This agrees with the paper's conclusion
that higher SRF activity marks insulin resistance, although none of these survive genome-wide
FDR on their own.

**Approaches that did not work, and why.** (1) Clustering on all variable genes produced
clusters with silhouette near 0, because between-subject biological differences are small
compared to array noise (median inter-sample r = `r round(median(medcor), 3)`). (2) Removing sex
genes did not reveal hidden structure, because sex was never the main driver. (3) Strict FDR
filtering gave no age genes, so a rank-based list had to be used, and pathway results from it
should be called exploratory. A better design would model age and glycemic status jointly,
use a larger cohort, or use gene-set methods (GSEA) that pool weak signals across many genes.

**Limitations.** Single time point, small groups (10 T2D), confounding between age and
diabetes, missing OGTT data for all T2D subjects, and two suspicious sample records.

# AI usage

Claude (Anthropic) was used to draft the analysis plan, write the R code in this R Markdown file,
and draft the text. The analysis choices (gene filtering, sex-gene removal, confounder
adjustment, outlier handling) and all interpretations were reviewed and checked against the
output by the author. Code was run in a GitHub Codespace / GitHub Actions runner (rocker/verse container).
